questions.title: Tuple Unpack and Swap
questions.objective: Unpack coordinates and swap endpoints using tuple assignment.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A line segment has two endpoints, start and end. Each endpoint is a point (x, y), stored as a tuple.

Read the two endpoints, build the segment as a tuple of two tuples, swap the endpoints, and print the results.
• Build start = (x1, y1) and end = (x2, y2), then segment = (start, end)
• Unpack the segment into two variables with one tuple assignment: start, end = segment
• Swap them with one tuple assignment: start, end = end, start (no temporary variable)
• Print the swapped segment (end first, then start) as a tuple
• On a second line, print the x value of the new start point and the y value of the new end point, separated by a space. Get them by unpacking: x, y = start

Example: for the endpoints 1 2 and 5 7 the output is
((5, 7), (1, 2))
5 2

Given the two endpoints, print the swapped segment.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: two integers x1 and y1 (the start point).
Line 2: two integers x2 and y2 (the end point).
questions.output_format:
Line 1: the swapped segment printed as a Python tuple: ((x2, y2), (x1, y1)).
Line 2: the x of the new start point and the y of the new end point, separated by a space.
hints: x1, y1 = map(int, input().split()) reads two numbers in one line.
a, b = b, a swaps two variables in Python without a temporary variable.
Printing a tuple directly gives the Python format: print((start, end)).
questions.reference_solution:
x1, y1 = map(int, input().split())
x2, y2 = map(int, input().split())

segment = ((x1, y1), (x2, y2))

start, end = segment          # tuple unpacking
start, end = end, start       # swap with one tuple assignment

print((start, end))

start_x, start_y = start
end_x, end_y = end
print(start_x, end_y)

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: two integers x1 and y1 (the start point).
Line 2: two integers x2 and y2 (the end point).
extra_fields.output_format:
Line 1: the swapped segment printed as a Python tuple: ((x2, y2), (x1, y1)).
Line 2: the x of the new start point and the y of the new end point, separated by a space.

questions.title: Set Membership Deduplicator
questions.objective: Print unique values from space-separated input stream using sets.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A set stores each value only once, and checking whether a value is in a set (x in seen) is very fast.

Read a line of integers and print every value once, in the order of its first appearance. Then print how many different values there are.
• Keep a set called seen with the values you have already printed
• Go through the numbers. If a number is not in seen, add it to the result and to seen
• A set has no order, so do not print the set itself: print the result list
• On the second line, print the number of different values. len(set(nums)) gives it directly

Example: for 4 2 4 9 2 4 the output is
4 2 9
3

Given a line of integers, print the unique values and their count.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format:
Line 1: the unique values in first-appearance order, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the number of unique values.
hints: seen = set() creates an empty set. Note that {} creates an empty dict, not a set.
Use if x not in seen: then seen.add(x) and result.append(x).
len(seen) at the end is the number of unique values.
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]

seen = set()
result = []

for x in nums:
    if x not in seen:
        seen.add(x)
        result.append(x)

print(" ".join(str(x) for x in result))
print(len(seen))

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format:
Line 1: the unique values in first-appearance order, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the number of unique values.

questions.title: Set Algebraic Operations
questions.objective: Print intersection, union, and symmetric difference counts.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Python sets support set algebra with operators:
• a & b is the intersection: values in both sets
• a | b is the union: values in at least one set
• a ^ b is the symmetric difference: values in exactly one of the sets

Read two lines of integers, turn each line into a set, and print the sizes of the intersection, the union and the symmetric difference. Repeated numbers inside one line count once, because they go into a set.

Example: for 1 2 3 4 and 3 4 5 the intersection is {3, 4}, the union is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and the symmetric difference is {1, 2, 5}, so the output is 2 5 3.

Given the two lines, print the three counts.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the integers of the first group, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integers of the second group, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line: the size of the intersection, the union and the symmetric difference, separated by single spaces.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of integers on each line <= 10^5
-10^9 <= each integer <= 10^9
hints: set(int(x) for x in input().split()) builds a set from one line.
Use the operators &, | and ^ (or the methods intersection, union, symmetric_difference).
len() gives the size of a set. print(a, b, c) puts single spaces between the three values.
questions.reference_solution:
s1 = set(int(x) for x in input().split())
s2 = set(int(x) for x in input().split())

common = s1 & s2        # intersection
combined = s1 | s2      # union
only_one = s1 ^ s2      # symmetric difference

print(len(common), len(combined), len(only_one))

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the integers of the first group, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integers of the second group, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the size of the intersection, the union and the symmetric difference, separated by single spaces.

questions.title: Tuple as Dict Coordinate Key
questions.objective: Store and retrieve elevations in dictionary using (x, y) tuples as keys.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Dictionary keys must be immutable. Lists cannot be keys, but tuples can, so a point (row, col) is a perfect key.

Read a map of elevations and store it in a dictionary whose keys are (row, col) tuples. Then answer queries about single points.
• The map has R rows and C columns. Rows and columns are numbered from 0
• Store each elevation as elevation[(row, col)] = value
• For each query point (row, col), print its elevation
• If the point is outside the map, print NOT FOUND. Use elevation.get(...) or the in operator instead of crashing with a KeyError

Example: for the 2 x 3 map
5 8 2
7 1 9
the query 1 2 prints 9, and the query 2 0 prints NOT FOUND.

Given the map and the queries, print one answer per query.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: two integers R and C.
Next R lines: the C elevations of one row, separated by single spaces.
Next line: the number of queries Q.
Next Q lines: two integers row and col.
questions.output_format: Q lines: the elevation at the query point, or NOT FOUND if the point is not on the map.
hints: Loop over the rows with enumerate to know the row number, and over the values with enumerate to know the column number.
Write elevation[(r, c)] = value. A tuple is hashable, so it can be a key.
elevation.get((row, col), 'NOT FOUND') returns the default when the key is missing.

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: two integers R and C.
Next R lines: the C elevations of one row, separated by single spaces.
Next line: the number of queries Q.
Next Q lines: two integers row and col.
extra_fields.output_format: Q lines: the elevation at the query point, or NOT FOUND if the point is not on the map.

questions.title: Word Count Frequency
questions.objective: Compute word frequency counts from tokens, building a dictionary.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a line of words and count how many times each word appears, using a dictionary.
• Words are separated by spaces
• Counting is not case-sensitive: The and the are the same word, so convert every word to lower case first
• The dictionary maps each word to its count: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
• Do not import collections.Counter
• Print one line per different word, in the order each word first appears: word: count

Example: for the line The cat and the hat the output is
the: 2
cat: 1
and: 1
hat: 1

Given a line of words, print the word counts.
questions.input_format: A single line containing words separated by spaces.
questions.output_format: One line for every different word, in first-appearance order: <word>: <count>
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of words <= 10^4
Words contain only English letters
hints: input().split() gives the list of words. Use word.lower() for each one.
counts.get(word, 0) gives 0 when the word is not in the dictionary yet.
A dict remembers the order in which keys were added, so for word, count in counts.items() gives first-appearance order.

test_cases.input: To be or not to be
x y z x y x

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing words separated by spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line for every different word, in first-appearance order: <word>: <count>

questions.title: Sort Tuples by Secondary Key
questions.objective: Sort tuples primarily by score descending, secondarily by age ascending.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Each student record is a tuple (name, score, age). Read the records and print them sorted:
• Higher score first (score descending)
• If two students have the same score, the younger one comes first (age ascending)
• If score and age are both equal, keep the input order (Python's sort is stable)

Use sorted() with a key function that returns a tuple. Tuples are compared item by item, so key=lambda rec: (-rec[1], rec[2]) sorts by score descending and then by age ascending.

Example: for the records
Asha 90 20
Ben 85 19
Chen 90 18
the output is
Chen 90 18
Asha 90 20
Ben 85 19

Given the records, print them in sorted order.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of records N.
Next N lines: name score age, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: N lines: the records in sorted order, each as name score age.
questions.constraints:
1 <= N <= 10^4
Names have no spaces
0 <= score <= 100
1 <= age <= 120
hints: Store each record as a tuple: (name, int(score), int(age)).
A minus sign in front of the score turns descending into ascending: key=lambda rec: (-rec[1], rec[2]).
Unpack each sorted record in the print loop: for name, score, age in ordered:.
questions.reference_solution:
n = int(input())

records = []
for _ in range(n):
    name, score, age = input().split()
    records.append((name, int(score), int(age)))

# score descending (minus sign), then age ascending
ordered = sorted(records, key=lambda rec: (-rec[1], rec[2]))

for name, score, age in ordered:
    print(name, score, age)

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the number of records N.
Next N lines: name score age, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: N lines: the records in sorted order, each as name score age.

questions.title: Invert Dictionary with Collisions
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Inverting a dictionary swaps keys and values: {k: v} becomes {v: k}. When several keys share the same value, they collide, so the inverted dictionary stores a LIST of keys for each value.

Read N key-value pairs into a dictionary d, then build the inverted dictionary {value: sorted list of keys}.
• All keys are different. Values may repeat
• The list of keys for each value must be sorted alphabetically
• Print one line per value, with the values in alphabetical order: value: key1 key2 ...

Example: for the pairs apple red, cherry red, banana yellow the dictionary is {'apple': 'red', 'cherry': 'red', 'banana': 'yellow'} and the output is
red: apple cherry
yellow: banana

Given the pairs, print the inverted dictionary.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of pairs N.
Next N lines: a key and a value separated by a single space.
questions.output_format: One line for every different value, in alphabetical order of the values: <value>: <keys in alphabetical order, separated by single spaces>
questions.constraints:
1 <= N <= 10^4
Keys and values are words without spaces
All keys are different
sample_inputs:
3
apple red
cherry red
banana yellow
hints: First read the pairs into d with d[key] = value.
For each key, value in d.items(): if value is not in inverted yet, start it with an empty list, then append the key. setdefault(value, []) does both steps.
Sort each list of keys, and loop over sorted(inverted) to print the values in order.

questions.title: Category Aggregator
questions.objective: Group items from (category, amount) tuples and compute category totals.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read N spending records. Each record is a (category, amount) tuple. Group the records by category with a dictionary and add up the amounts.
• totals[category] holds the sum of all amounts in that category
• Print one line per category, in the order each category first appears: category total
• After the categories, print one more line: TOTAL followed by the sum of all amounts

Example: for the records food 120, travel 300, food 80 the output is
food 200
travel 300
TOTAL 500

Given the records, print the totals.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of records N.
Next N lines: a category and an integer amount separated by a single space.
questions.output_format: One line per category in first-appearance order: <category> <total>, then a last line: TOTAL <sum of all amounts>.
questions.constraints:
1 <= N <= 10^5
Categories are words without spaces
0 <= amount <= 10^6
hints: Store each record as a tuple (category, amount) in a list first.
Unpack in the loop: for category, amount in records:, then totals[category] = totals.get(category, 0) + amount.
sum(totals.values()) gives the grand total.

6
c 1
b 2
a 3
c 4
b 5
a 6

Line 1: the number of records N.
Next N lines: a category and an integer amount separated by a single space.
extra_fields.output_format: One line per category in first-appearance order: <category> <total>, then a last line: TOTAL <sum of all amounts>.

questions.title: Dense Rank Calculator
questions.objective: Assign dense ranks to integer scores using set sorting and dict lookup.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: In dense ranking, the highest score gets rank 1, the next different score gets rank 2, and so on. Equal scores share the same rank, and there are no gaps between ranks.

Read a list of scores and print the dense rank of each score, in the input order.
• Put the scores in a set to remove repeats, then sort the set from highest to lowest
• Build a dictionary rank_of that maps each different score to its rank (1, 2, 3, ...)
• Look up the rank of every score in the dictionary

Example: for 100 90 90 80 100 the different scores in order are 100, 90, 80, so the output is 1 2 2 3 1.

Given the scores, print their dense ranks.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the scores, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line: the dense rank of each score in input order, separated by single spaces.
hints: sorted(set(scores), reverse=True) gives the different scores from highest to lowest.
Use enumerate(..., start=1) to give the ranks: rank_of[score] = rank.
A dict lookup takes O(1) time, so [rank_of[s] for s in scores] is fast.
questions.reference_solution:
scores = [int(x) for x in input().split()]

unique_desc = sorted(set(scores), reverse=True)

rank_of = {}
for rank, score in enumerate(unique_desc, start=1):
    rank_of[score] = rank

ranks = [rank_of[s] for s in scores]
print(" ".join(str(r) for r in ranks))

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the scores, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the dense rank of each score in input order, separated by single spaces.

questions.title: Two-Sum Hash Map Lookup
questions.objective: Find pair of indices summing to target in O(N) using a dictionary.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a list of integers and a target. Find two different positions i < j such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target, in one pass with a dictionary.
• Go through the list from left to right with index j
• For each nums[j], the partner it needs is target - nums[j]. If that partner was seen before, its index i is in the dictionary: print i j and stop
• Otherwise store nums[j] in the dictionary as value -> index. Store only the FIRST index of each value (do not overwrite it)
• This finds the pair with the smallest possible j, and for that j the smallest i
• If there is no such pair, print NOT FOUND
• Positions start at 0

Example: for the list 2 7 11 15 and target 9 the output is 0 1.

Given the list and the target, print the pair of indices.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the integers, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the target integer.
questions.output_format: One line: the indices i and j separated by a single space, or NOT FOUND.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of integers <= 10^5
-10^9 <= each integer, target <= 10^9
hints: first_index = {} maps a value to the first position where it appeared.
Check need = target - nums[j] with if need in first_index BEFORE storing nums[j]. This stops a number from pairing with itself.
Use a found flag and break, then print NOT FOUND after the loop if nothing was found.
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]
target = int(input())

first_index = {}
found = False

for j, value in enumerate(nums):
    need = target - value
    if need in first_index:
        print(first_index[need], j)
        found = True
        break
    if value not in first_index:      # keep only the first index
        first_index[value] = j

if not found:
    print("NOT FOUND")

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the integers, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the target integer.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the indices i and j separated by a single space, or NOT FOUND.

questions.title: First Unique Character
questions.objective: Identify first non-repeating character in string in O(N).
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a string and print its first character that appears exactly once.
• Characters are case-sensitive: a and A are different characters
• First count every character with a dictionary in one pass over the string
• A dict keeps the order in which keys were first added, so the first key with count 1 is the answer. You do not need a second pass over the whole string
• If every character repeats, print NONE

Examples: for leetcode the output is l. For loveleetcode the output is v. For aabb the output is NONE.

Given a string, print its first unique character.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the string (no spaces).
questions.output_format: One line: the first non-repeating character, or NONE if there is none.
questions.constraints:
1 <= length of the string <= 10^5
The string has no spaces
hints: counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1 for every character ch.
for ch, count in counts.items(): goes through the characters in first-appearance order.
Print the first ch with count == 1 and break. Use a flag (or for ... else) to print NONE when there is none.

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the string (no spaces).
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the first non-repeating character, or NONE if there is none.

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K (O(N))
questions.objective: Count subarrays summing to K using prefix sum frequencies in dict.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A subarray is a continuous part of a list. Read a list of integers and a number k, and count how many subarrays have a sum equal to k.

The O(N) method uses prefix sums. The prefix sum at position j is the sum of nums[0] to nums[j]. The subarray from i + 1 to j has sum prefix[j] - prefix[i]. So a subarray ending at j has sum k exactly when an earlier prefix sum equals prefix[j] - k.
• Keep a dictionary seen that maps each prefix sum to how many times it has appeared. Start with seen = {0: 1} for the empty prefix
• Walk through the list, update the running sum, add seen.get(running - k, 0) to the answer, then record the running sum in seen
• Numbers can be negative, so the sliding-window trick does not work here

Example: for the list 1 1 1 and k = 2 the output is 2 (the subarrays [1, 1] at positions 0-1 and 1-2).

Given the list and k, print the number of subarrays.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the integers, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integer k.
questions.output_format: One integer: the number of subarrays whose sum is k.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of integers <= 10^5
-1000 <= each integer <= 1000
-10^7 <= k <= 10^7
hints: Start with running = 0, count = 0 and seen = {0: 1}.
For each x: running += x, then count += seen.get(running - k, 0).
Only after that, do seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1. The order matters.
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]
k = int(input())

seen = {0: 1}      # prefix sum -> how many times it appeared
running = 0
count = 0

for x in nums:
    running += x
    # an earlier prefix equal to running - k gives a subarray with sum k
    count += seen.get(running - k, 0)
    seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1

print(count)

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the integers, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integer k.
extra_fields.output_format: One integer: the number of subarrays whose sum is k.

questions.title: Find Disappeared Numbers
questions.objective: Find all integers missing from [1, N] using set difference.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a list of N integers. Every number is between 1 and N, but some numbers may appear more than once, so some numbers from 1 to N are missing. Print the missing numbers.
• Build the set of all numbers from 1 to N: set(range(1, n + 1))
• Build the set of numbers that appear in the list
• The missing numbers are the set difference: full - present
• Print them in increasing order
• If no number is missing, print NONE

Example: for 4 3 2 7 8 2 3 1 (N = 8) the output is 5 6.

Given the list, print the missing numbers.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the N integers, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line: the missing numbers in increasing order separated by single spaces, or NONE.
hints: N is the number of integers: n = len(nums).
The - operator on two sets gives the values in the first set but not in the second.
A set has no order, so print sorted(missing).
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]
n = len(nums)

full = set(range(1, n + 1))
present = set(nums)
missing = sorted(full - present)     # set difference

if missing:
    print(" ".join(str(x) for x in missing))
else:
    print("NONE")

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the N integers, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the missing numbers in increasing order separated by single spaces, or NONE.

questions.title: Deep Merge Dictionaries
questions.objective: Merge two nested dictionaries at every level with dict2 overrides.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read two dictionaries d1 and d2, written as Python dictionary literals, and print their deep merge.

A normal d1.update(d2) replaces a nested dictionary completely. A deep merge goes inside nested dictionaries:
• For every key in d2: if the key is in d1 AND both values are dictionaries, merge those two dictionaries in the same way (at every depth)
• Otherwise the value from d2 replaces (or adds) the value in d1. Lists and other values are replaced, not merged
• Keys keep the order of d1, and new keys from d2 are added at the end, in d2's order (this is what assigning to a dict does)

Instead of a recursive function, use a stack: a list of (target, source) dictionary pairs that still need merging. Start with [(d1, d2)]. Pop a pair, copy the keys of source into target, and push any nested dictionary pairs you meet.

Example: for d1 = {'a': 1, 'cfg': {'x': 1, 'y': 2}} and d2 = {'cfg': {'y': 20, 'z': 30}, 'b': 2} the output is
{'a': 1, 'cfg': {'x': 1, 'y': 20, 'z': 30}, 'b': 2}

Given d1 and d2, print the merged dictionary.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the dictionary d1 as a Python literal.
Line 2: the dictionary d2 as a Python literal.
Read each line with ast.literal_eval(input()). Keys are strings. Values are integers, strings, lists or dictionaries.
questions.output_format: One line: the merged dictionary, printed as a Python dict.
questions.constraints:
Each dictionary has at most 1000 keys in total, over all levels
Nesting depth <= 20
hints: import ast, then ast.literal_eval(input()) safely turns the text {'a': 1} into a real dict.
isinstance(value, dict) checks whether a value is a dictionary.
Use stack = [(d1, d2)] and while stack: target, source = stack.pop(). When both target[key] and source[key] are dicts, push (target[key], source[key]); otherwise do target[key] = source[key].

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the dictionary d1 as a Python literal.
Line 2: the dictionary d2 as a Python literal.
Read each line with ast.literal_eval(input()). Keys are strings. Values are integers, strings, lists or dictionaries.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the merged dictionary, printed as a Python dict.

questions.title: Group Anagrams via Tuples
questions.objective: Group strings into anagrams using sorted character tuples as dict keys.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Two words are anagrams if they use exactly the same letters the same number of times, like eat and tea. If you sort the letters of anagrams, you get the same result.

Read a list of words and group the anagrams together.
• For each word, build the key tuple(sorted(word)). A tuple can be a dict key, but a list cannot
• Use a dictionary that maps each key to the list of words with that key
• Print one group per line, words separated by spaces
• Print the groups in the order their first word appears in the input, and keep the input order inside each group
• Comparison is case-sensitive, and repeated words stay in the group as many times as they appear

Example: for eat tea tan ate nat bat the output is
eat tea ate
tan nat
bat

Given the words, print the anagram groups.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the words, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line per anagram group: the words of the group separated by single spaces.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of words <= 10^4
1 <= length of each word <= 100
Words contain only English letters
sample_inputs: eat tea tan ate nat bat
sample_outputs:
eat tea ate
tan nat
bat
hints: sorted('tea') gives ['a', 'e', 't']. Wrap it with tuple() so it can be a dict key.
groups.setdefault(key, []).append(word) creates the list the first time and appends every time.

questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.objective: Find K most frequent elements in O(N log N) using hash map and sort.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a list of integers and a number k, and print the k values that appear most often.
• Count every value with a dictionary
• Sort the different values by count, highest first. If two values have the same count, the smaller value comes first
• Print the first k values of that order
• k is never bigger than the number of different values

Use sorted() with a tuple key: key=lambda v: (-counts[v], v).

Example: for the list 1 1 1 2 2 3 and k = 2 the output is 1 2.

Given the list and k, print the k most frequent values.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the integers, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integer k.
questions.output_format: One line: the k most frequent values (highest count first, smaller value first on ties), separated by single spaces.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of integers <= 10^5
-10^4 <= each integer <= 10^4
1 <= k <= number of different values
hints: counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1 for every x.
sorted(counts, key=lambda v: (-counts[v], v)) sorts the different values: count descending, then value ascending.
Slice the sorted list with [:k] and print it joined with spaces.
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]
k = int(input())

counts = {}
for x in nums:
    counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1

# highest count first; on a tie, the smaller value first
ordered = sorted(counts, key=lambda v: (-counts[v], v))

print(" ".join(str(v) for v in ordered[:k]))

Line 2: the integer k.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the k most frequent values (highest count first, smaller value first on ties), separated by single spaces.
